title: Call Schema Annotation Runtime and Diagnostic Envelope
creator: Priya Natarajan
description: Define and implement a runtime annotation format and diagnostic envelope for function/tool calling that produces deterministic validation results, human- and machine-readable error messages, and graceful compatibility shims across older SDKs and model variants.
background: Customers embed structured tool schemas in prompts or model manifests. Today our runtime performs ad-hoc JSON validation and returns opaque errors or model-text rejections. This leads to user confusion, high debugging time for integrators, and fragile fallback behavior when models emit slightly wrong shapes. We need a formal annotation format for schema semantics (required vs recommended, coercion modes, severity levels) plus an error envelope with canonical codes, localization-friendly messages, and sparse telemetry hooks.
goals: Design a small, annotation-first JSON schema extension for function/tool parameters that signals requiredness, recommended fields, coercion policy, and deprecation notes
Implement runtime validator that emits canonical error codes and a structured diagnostic envelope consumable by Console and SDKs
Introduce compatibility shims (coercion strategies) controlled by per-route policy and annotated in the manifest
Ship end-to-end tests and a migration guide for model teams and SDK authors
non_goals: Rewriting the full OpenAPI/JSON Schema spec support set (we only support a small safe subset)
Full localization of all error messages in first release
Changes to model training or generation policies
acceptance_criteria: Runtime can parse and honor annotation fields: 'required', 'recommend', 'coerce', 'severity', 'deprecation'
Validator returns diagnostic envelope with fields: code, path, severity, message, suggestion, raw_example where applicable
SDKs (js/py) display SDK-friendly error messages mapped from diagnostic envelope codes
Console surface shows per-route validation failure counts and sample diagnostics
Backward compatibility: when 'coerce' is 'lenient' runtime tolerates common shape mismatches (string->number, single->array) and emits a lower-severity diagnostic
Automated test coverage: unit tests for 45 validation scenarios and end-to-end integration test with mock model emitting invalid JSON
implementation_notes: Annotation syntax: small extension keys placed under 'x-rw-annotations' on the parameter definition object
Validator flow: parse -> fast schema check -> shape coercion (if allowed) -> semantic check -> emit envelope
Coercion modes: strict (no coercion), lenient (string->number, single->array), safe-coerce (only lossless conversions)
Diagnostic envelope codes follow pattern RW.VAL.<DOMAIN>.<TYPE> e.g., RW.VAL.PARAM.MISSING, RW.VAL.PARAM.TYPE_MISMATCH
Telemetry events: validation.failure and validation.coercion_applied with route_id, model_variant, annotation_id
Config knobs: per-route validation_level: off | warn | error and per-customer default in Dedicated/Private
design_tradeoffs: We avoid full JSON Schema to reduce runtime complexity; tradeoff is less expressivity for authors but faster validation and clearer errors
Placing annotations under a vendor-prefixed key keeps host schema compatibility but requires SDK/author education
Lenient coercion reduces friction but may mask upstream model issues; therefore coercion emits lower-severity diagnostics and is opt-in per-route
detailed_plan: Week 0: RFC and annotation spec review with API, Runtime, SDK, and Console owners
Week 1: Implement in-runtime parser and fast type checks, add coercion helpers
Week 2: Implement diagnostic envelope generator and map codes to human messages
Week 3: SDK mappings (js/py) and Console ingestion + storage for sample diagnostics
Week 4: Test hardening, integration tests with mock model, rollout to canary routes
Week 5: Gradual rollout to hosted with feature flag, docs and migration guide publication
testing_plan: Unit tests for each coercion rule and severity mapping
Property tests that random valid inputs remain accepted when coercion enabled
E2E test where mock model emits malformed JSON and we validate envelope creation and SDK display
Performance benchmark: validate < 350 microseconds p50 for a typical 12-field schema on a 4-core runtime shard
Chaos test: ensure no regressions when validator throws; fallback to model-text parsing with 'validation_level: warn'
monitoring_and_telemetry: Tag events with route_id, model_version, customer_tier
Console shows top 10 diagnostic codes by route in last 7 days
Add alert: if validation.failures.rate increases > 3x baseline for a route, create SRE paging alert (P1)
rollout_strategy: Enable in Dedicated as an opt-in cluster parameter; provide migration audit reports
Private installs receive migration bundle and CLI verifier
Canary small subset of routes for 48h, review telemetry, then widen to 10% of routes before full rollout
risks: Users may misuse 'lenient' coercion causing silent data corruption; mitigated by audit logs and defaulting to 'strict' for new routes
Performance regression if validation not optimized; mitigated by microbenchmarks and fast-path skip when annotation absent
Interoperability issues with legacy SDKs; mitigated by clear SDK mapping and version gate
open_questions: Should 'recommend' fields be surfaced differently in Console UX than 'required'?
Do we allow custom vendor codes in the diagnostic envelope or reserve the RW.VAL namespace only?
What's the minimal set of coercions we accept for first release without increasing support load?
deliverables: Runtime validator implementation and benchmark results
SDK error mapping PRs (js and py)
Console diagnostic ingestion + UI surface for sample diagnostics
